title: The Prince and the Pebble
hook: a prince sets a trap, a baby on his lap gives the answer, and a neighbor's poem about seasons
carry: right speech: true, helpful, then the right time
tomorrow: what changes when you listen without loading your reply?

segments.voice: Yesterday, kind at home: Vedehika was gentle only until someone pushed. Today, words that are true and still might land wrong.

A friend's bad haircut, pointed out the night before her school photo. A brother's grade, announced at the dinner table. An apology, ready to go, while the person who needs it is asleep on the couch. True, all three. So is a true thing, said at the wrong moment, still right speech? A prince once tried to trap the Buddha with that question, and a baby sitting on the prince's lap gave the answer.
screen: `TRUE, ALL THREE.` → `STILL RIGHT SPEECH?` → `A BABY ON THE PRINCE'S LAP.`

segments.voice: Prince Abhaya came with a trick question: would you ever say something unwelcome? Say yes, and you're as harsh as anyone. Say no, and explain the hard things you've said. The Buddha looked at the baby on Abhaya's lap. If your child put a pebble in his mouth, what would you do? I'd get it out, the prince said, even if it drew a little blood. Because I love him. So the Buddha sorted words three ways: true or not, helpful or not, welcome or not. Untrue, he doesn't say. True but unhelpful, he doesn't say. True and helpful, welcome or not, he knows the right time to say it. Timing is the last check, after truth and help. Now a neighbor. In Ecclesiastes, a book Jews and Christians share, comes a poem of seasons. In the King James words: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven," and among them, "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak." Shared ground: both see that silence and speech each have their hour. One honest difference: in Ecclesiastes the times are set under heaven, and a few verses on, God "hath made every thing beautiful in his time." The Buddha's version is a judgment the speaker makes, after two other checks. Neither text says the hard words go unsaid forever. Both say: wait for the hour, then speak.
screen: `A TRICK QUESTION.` · `A PEBBLE IN THE BABY'S MOUTH.` · `TRUE, HELPFUL, THEN THE MOMENT.` · `A TIME TO SPEAK, IN ECCLESIASTES.` · then, large: `THE RIGHT TIME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one true thing you need to say to someone close. Ask it the three questions slowly: is it true, is it helpful, and when could they actually hear it? Settle on the moment, maybe tomorrow at breakfast, maybe a walk this weekend, and let the words wait there, ready, until it comes.
The right time: the last check on true, helpful words. In Pali, kala, time; in MN 58 the Buddha knows the time to speak.
Keep this one close: right speech is true, then helpful, then said at the right time. Two of four, on speech at home.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often teach right speech with MN 58's checks (true, beneficial, and the right time); Jews and Christians read the seasons poem of Ecclesiastes 3, which is sometimes read at weddings and funerals.

fork.setup: your best friend's sketch for the art show has a mistake, and she doesn't see it. it's true and it would help. the show is in a week. what does MN 58 point to?
options: say nothing; unwelcome words aren't right speech.
tell her right now, in front of the group, since it's true.
tell her, at a moment she can hear it and still fix it.
fork.reveal: true and helpful words, even unwelcome, the Buddha says at the right time. here the right time is soon, in private, while she can still fix it.

what a scholar hears: MN 58, the Abhayarajakumara Sutta, sorts speech by truth, benefit and welcome, and says the Tathagata knows the time to speak; the baby-and-pebble simile is its center.

chat.says: want to say sorry rn but mom got home from a 12-hr shift and she's half asleep. now or wait?
options: It's true and kind, so say it. Just pick a moment she can actually hear it.
Now. A true apology is right whenever you say it; timing doesn't matter.
Skip it. If it might be unwelcome tonight, the Buddha wouldn't say it.
chat.meaning: In MN 58, true and helpful words get said, at the right time. An apology passes the first two checks; timing is the last.

tie.story: The Buddha said true, helpful words even when unwelcome, but always at the right time.
tie.friend: Mai's apology is true and helpful; she can say it when her mom is awake enough to hear it.
tie.you: what true thing are you holding, waiting for its moment?

notes: Wisdom shape, unity thread: shared ground with the Jewish and Christian neighbor (Ecclesiastes 3, KJV) is that silence and speech each have their time; the honest difference is that Ecclesiastes sets the times under heaven, made beautiful by God, while MN 58 makes timing the speaker's judgment after truth and benefit. No ranking. Confirm the framing with Keepers on both sides.
